title: Types of RAG: corrective, agentic, graph and more
question: What are corrective, self, agentic, graph, multimodal and adaptive RAG?

steps.caption: The interviewer sets the problem.

problem.statement: Better search isn’t always enough. Some answers need the system to *check its own work*, take *several steps*, or understand how documents *connect*. Which RAG types handle that?
example: A legal assistant where a wrong answer is costly
“Compare our churn with the industry and explain why”
“What are the main themes across 10,000 support tickets?”
constraints: Each extra check costs time and money
Wrong answers must be rare, and explainable
problem.followUp: How do you stop a smart RAG system from looping forever or costing too much?

steps.caption: What the interviewer is really asking.

plain.asking: These types add *thinking around the search*: checking results, deciding when to search, planning steps, or reading across documents.
points: *You get:* harder questions than one search can answer.
*You do:* match each type to the failure it prevents.
*The catch:* more thinking means more cost and more delay.

steps.caption: Plain RAG trusts whatever search returns. Ask about something your documents barely cover, and the AI still gets weak chunks and builds an answer from them.

items.label: GRADER
items.note: A small model that scores how well each chunk answers the question.

steps.caption: Corrective RAG (CRAG) adds a *grader*: a small model that scores each retrieved chunk. Good chunks pass through. Weak ones are dropped.

items.label: GRADER
items.note: A small model that scores how well each chunk answers the question.

steps.caption: The paper’s grader gives one of three verdicts: *correct* (keep the chunks), *incorrect* (throw them out and search the web instead), or *unsure* (do both).

items.label: GRADER
items.note: A small model that scores how well each chunk answers the question.

steps.caption: Use it where a wrong answer is costly: legal or policy research, anything beyond your index. The price is an extra model call and a slower answer.
Your turn.

check.question: Retrieval returns only weak chunks for a question your documents don’t cover. What does Corrective RAG do?
options: Grades the chunks and falls back to a web search
Answers from the weak chunks anyway
check.explain: The grader notices the chunks are weak, so instead of trusting them it *drops them and searches elsewhere*. That is the “corrective” part.

steps.eyebrow: Does it need to look up at all?
steps.caption: “What is 12 × 12?” needs no documents. Self-RAG teaches the model to *decide for itself* when to retrieve, so it skips pointless searches.

items.label: THE MODEL DECIDES
items.note: In Self-RAG the model itself learns to emit a “retrieve” token when it needs outside facts.

labels.text: “What did our Q3 report say about churn?”  →  LOOK IT UP

steps.caption: It then critiques itself with special tokens: *Look up? Passage relevant? My claim supported? Answer useful?* Weak sentences get redone.

labels.text: DO I NEED TO LOOK THIS UP?

steps.caption: It suits assistants where most questions don’t need documents and citations matter. Catch: the original design trains the model itself, so it is harder to adopt.

labels.text: BEST FOR: MIXED CHAT + CITED ANSWERS
COST: NEEDS A SPECIALLY TRAINED MODEL

steps.caption: “Compare our churn with the industry, and explain why.” That is three questions in one: our number, theirs, and the reasons. A single search can’t answer it.

labels.text: ONE SEARCH → ONE PIECE OF THE ANSWER ✕

steps.caption: Agentic RAG lets the AI act as an *agent*. It plans: (1) our churn, (2) the industry’s churn, (3) the reasons. Then it picks a tool for each.

items.label: AGENT · PLANS AND DECIDES
items.note: An LLM in a loop: pick a tool, read the result, decide whether it knows enough.

steps.caption: First it asks the SQL database: “churn last quarter?” The answer, 4.1%, goes back to the agent, which reads it and decides what to do next.

items.label: AGENT · PLANS AND DECIDES
items.note: An LLM in a loop: pick a tool, read the result, decide whether it knows enough.

steps.caption: Next it searches the web for the industry average, then the documents for customer complaints. Each result decides the next move.

items.label: AGENT · PLANS AND DECIDES
items.note: An LLM in a loop: pick a tool, read the result, decide whether it knows enough.

steps.caption: With all three pieces, the agent writes the comparison and the likely causes. A *step limit* stops it looping, since every extra loop costs time and money.

items.label: AGENT · PLANS AND DECIDES
items.note: An LLM in a loop: pick a tool, read the result, decide whether it knows enough.

labels.text: “Churn is 0.9 pts above industry; top complaint: billing.”

steps.caption: It suits research and due-diligence questions that need several sources. The cost is real: slower, pricier, and harder to debug than one search.

labels.text: COST: SLOWER · PRICIER · HARDER TO DEBUG

steps.caption: Your turn.

check.question: Why cap an agent at a maximum number of steps?
options: To stop endless loops and runaway cost
check.explain: An agent decides for itself when it is done. Without a limit, a confused one can loop forever, so the cap is a *safety net* for time and money.

steps.caption: “What are the main themes across 10,000 support tickets?” Vector search returns the 5 most similar chunks, which tells you nothing about the *whole* pile.
Graph RAG has an AI read everything once and pull out *entities* (people, companies, products) and *relationships*, building a map of what connects to what.
An algorithm groups tightly connected nodes into *communities*, and an AI writes a short summary of each. Microsoft’s GraphRAG works this way.
To answer “what are the main themes?”, the AI reads the *community summaries* instead of raw chunks. They already cover the whole pile.
Graph RAG also answers “how is Ana connected to Bank?” by following links, which similarity search can’t do. Great for fraud rings and investigations.

labels.text: USE CASE: FRAUD, INVESTIGATIONS, RESEARCH LITERATURE

steps.caption: It shines on questions about the whole collection or about connections. The cost: heavy indexing (many AI calls) and a rebuild whenever the data changes much.

labels.text: COST: HEAVY INDEXING · REBUILD ON CHANGE

steps.caption: Your turn.

check.question: Which question suits Graph RAG best?
options: What are the main themes across all 10,000 tickets?
check.explain: A question about the *whole collection* can’t be answered from a few similar chunks. Graph RAG’s community summaries already cover everything.

steps.caption: A manual’s answer may be inside a chart, a diagram or a photo. Multimodal RAG indexes images and tables too, on the same map as text.

labels.text: USE CASE: EQUIPMENT MANUALS, MEDICAL REPORTS, SLIDE DECKS

steps.eyebrow: Two ways to index an image
steps.caption: Either embed the *image itself* with a multimodal model, or have an AI *describe it in words* and embed that. The retrieved image then goes to a vision-capable AI.

labels.text: COST: BIGGER INDEX · NEEDS A VISION MODEL

steps.caption: “Hi!” needs no search. “What is the refund window?” needs one. “Compare plans and costs” needs several. Adaptive RAG gauges the difficulty and picks the effort.

items.label: DIFFICULTY CHECK
items.note: A small model that judges how hard the question is.

steps.caption: It suits support bots that get every kind of question: easy ones stay cheap and fast. Catch: if the difficulty check misjudges, a hard question gets too little effort.

labels.text: BEST FOR: SUPPORT BOTS WITH MIXED QUESTIONS
COST: A MISJUDGED QUESTION GETS TOO LITTLE

steps.caption: Match the symptom to the type. Don’t add thinking you don’t need:

labels.text: IF QUESTIONS SPAN THE WHOLE PILE

steps.caption: And for the rest:

labels.text: IF NONE OF THE ABOVE HURTS

steps.caption: The big idea: *start with simple RAG and add only the type that fixes the failure you actually see.* More thinking always costs time and money.
